Our research marks the first successful recording of a Cherenkov cone in the soft X-ray spectrum through in-depth X-ray bremsstrahlung experiments. To achieve this, we employed a compact X-ray source generated by inverse Compton upconversion and a sapphire crystal bent crystal spectrometer tailored for X-ray angles as low as 16.8 degrees. The observed Cherenkov cone in soft X-rays is seen in a 4-μm thick beryllium target at an angle of 22.6 degrees, while in silicon targets, the phenomenon was observed at angles of 25.1° and 27.4°, corresponding to 10.5 and 18.2 microns of bremsstrahlahlung production.

This study provides a systematic approach to refining implicit argument annotations within UCCA, a linguistic annotation framework that represents sentence structures as a graph. By integrating a large corpus of annotated sentences with UCCA guidelines, we manually update a subset of the annotations and develop a method to produce annotations that align with UCCA's dependency tree and sentence pattern. Our method is based on the principles of UCCA's dependency scheme and sentence pattern, and it allows for the annotation process to be guided by both human effort and computational optimization.

A common approach to disease localization in radiology is Multiple Instance Learning, but this technique often fails when training data lacks sufficient supervision. In this study, we developed an innovative self-supervised method to address weakly supervised disease classification and localization on chest X-rays. Our approach, called Self-guided Multiple Instance Learning, leverages contrastive learning to extract and retain informative radii from each ROI, thus enhancing the representation capabilities of multiple instance training. In essence, our method combines the capabilities of multiple instance training and self-supervised learning, with the former retaining the representation capabilities of the latter. Experimental results on two public chest X-ray datasets demonstrate that our Self-Guided Multiple Instance Learning outperforms existing weakly supervised methods.

A novel approach to selecting the optimal penalized Hellinger distance is developed, which is a parameter estimation method applicable to discrete data sets. The traditional method of using sparsity prior information is limited in cases with small sample sizes, resulting in the risk of underestimating the number of signals. To address this, a new method is proposed that utilizes the eigenvalues of the covariance of the observed data. The method is supported by theoretical analysis, demonstrating its ability to accurately identify signals and the derivation of relevant inequalities. Simulation studies and a real-world example apply this approach to microarray data and show that it outperforms existing methods in signal estimation accuracy.

Our research confirms that patterns of binary digits appear at a consistent frequency in both the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence and its various subsequences. Furthermore, we establish a specific lower bound for the frequency of binary patterns in these sequences. We also investigate the length of the subsequences required to ensure that a specific binary pattern appears at least once within them.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to Dynamic Classifier Selection, a type of multi-classifier system, that focuses on the performance and cost of its decision-making process. It proposes a new algorithm, COTS, that efficiently combines multiple classifiers using hierarchical clustering to identify similar classifiers and reduce the complexity of the selection process. Additionally, a cost model is introduced to evaluate the expense of each classifier. Experimental results on 12 datasets demonstrate that our algorithm, COTS, outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed, offering significant improvements.

The Tianlai project involves establishing a network of 20 telescopes at various remote locations worldwide, each equipped with a 6-meter radio telescope. These telescopes will track the cosmic microwave background in a specific redshift range of 0.2 to 3.5. To achieve this, the project relies on a sophisticated data processing system that can handle multiple data streams from the telescopes in real-time. This system processes data through a hierarchical pipeline consisting of three distinct stages: real-time data analysis, offline data analysis, and archival data processing. Each stage encompasses a range of critical processes, including data validation, correction, and calibration. This paper delves into the real-time analysis component, focusing on the core software framework that enables real-time data processing at the Tianlai Array Center (TAC).

Recently, a family of monolayer compounds, comprising silicon or phosphorus with niobium or vanadium, has garnered interest, showcasing a unique, two-dimensional structure with a combination of hexagonal and trigonal prismatic atomic arrangements.  Theoretical studies have predicted that these compounds exhibit remarkable stability, with calculated band gaps surpassing 1.5 eV.  The study of their electronic and magnetic properties is crucial for understanding their potential applications in spintronics.  The current research investigates the electronic and magnetic characteristics of NbSi2N4, VSi2N4, and VSi2P4 monolayers, with calculations indicating that the first two compounds exhibit ferromagnetic ordering, while the third compound does not exhibit magnetic ordering.  The study also examines the impact of spin-orbit coupling on the compounds' electronic band structures, with van der Waals interactions found to have a negligible effect on their band gaps.  The study's findings suggest that the compounds' large band gaps make them suitable for use in spintronics applications, with the ferromagnetic ordering of NbSi2N4 and VSi2N4 providing a promising foundation for further research and development.

In this work, we develop positive definite functions on a metric space with a specific metric, allowing for the creation of stationary Gaussian processes on such spaces. Our method is based on a modified version of the Gneiting-Lange approach, originally designed for standard Euclidean spaces. Our unstructured coefficients ensure the validity of the resulting positive definite functions, with the option to impose additional constraints and generate more organized expressions by solving linear programming problems.

A subset within the set of nonnegative real numbers that is closed under addition is called a positive monoid. Such monoids can represent matrices with nonnegative entries forming a semigroup. This work explores atomic elements and prime elements within a positive monoid. An atomic element within a positive monoid must be irreducible, meaning it cannot be broken down further into two non-zero elements. This study's main findings are about the atomic elements and their connection to irreducible elements within a nonnegative monoid.

A statistical method, attributable fraction among the exposed (AFEx), is used to quantify the attributable risk associated with a specific risk factor. This method, however, has limitations as it only considers the risk factor's associated risk and overlooks other risk factors that contribute to the condition. This oversight can result in an underestimation of the true attributable risk due to confounding bias. To address this issue, researchers have proposed an alternative method called AFEx* which utilizes additional information about disease causes to account for additional risk factor associations. This method, however, relies on the assumption that case descriptions are randomly distributed within the population, a notion not always easily verified. To mitigate this limitation, researchers have suggested the use of randomization in stratification, a statistical approach that can reduce bias stemming from non-random disease causes. This method, however, can be challenging to implement in practice. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed an alternative method, called AFEx control, which utilizes case description information to adjust for bias and produce an AFEx estimate that is less sensitive to confounding bias. This method, however, can result in biased estimates if the case descriptions are not randomly distributed. To address this issue, researchers have proposed the use of a weighted AFEx control method, which can produce unbiased estimates if the case descriptions are randomly distributed within certain strata. This method, however, requires knowledge of the strata distribution. To address this issue, researchers have proposed the use of a data-driven method,

We establish the Riemann-Roch theorem for zero-cycles on normal varieties by deriving a result that facilitates the verification of the Bloch-Beilinson tangent obstruction. Furthermore, we prove the presence of the Bloch group within the unit equation for zero-cycles on regular surfaces when the surface's surface K\'ahler class contains an integral component.

Researchers have recorded 502 $\Upsilon$(1S) and 51 $\Upsilon$(2S) events, as well as 13 $\Upsilon$(3S) candidates in proton-proton collisions at the LHCb detector, with a 7 TeV centre-of-mass energy and a combined integrated luminosity of 0.36 pb$^{-1}$. The relative production rates of the states $\Upsilon$(1S), $\Upsilon$(2S), and $\Upsilon$(3S) have been found to vary with event activity, with the most significant change observed between the most and least active events, specifically with the ratio of $\Upsilon$(3S) to $\Upsilon$(1S) production increasing by a factor of 3.5, while the relative production of the states $\Upsilon$(1S) and $\Upsilon$(2S) shows little to no variation.

We have successfully measured the entropy of a confined quantum particle within a classical framework by analyzing its energy distribution. Our research, led by experimental findings and supported by theoretical evidence, demonstrates this approach's applicability to a quantum dot system. By calculating the entropy of a quantum dot from the measured momentum distribution, we were able to accurately compare it with the entropy generated through entropy splitting in a double quantum dot system.

The Geometric Modulus Principle of Kalantari defines how the value of a polynomial changes when moving along specific paths in the complex plane. We expand upon this concept, exploring its equivalent for holomorphic and harmonic functions within bounded regions of the complex plane. We demonstrate that the Geometric Modulus Principle can be applied to holomorphic functions within these regions, allowing us to express the change in modulus of a holomorphic function as a linear combination of the real and imaginary components of its value. Furthermore, when considering harmonic functions, the change in their modulus can be represented as a linear combination of their harmonic components. We also establish that the Geometric Modulus Principle has a corresponding principle for the boundary of regions where harmonic functions are zero. We use these principles to derive various bounds on the derivatives of holomorphic and harmonic functions within bounded regions.

We investigate the stability of soliton solutions to a discrete model of the cubic-quartic nonlinear Schrodinger equation, incorporating long-range dipole-dipole interactions. Our research reveals that such interactions can both stabilise and lead to the collapse of stable solitons arising in the underlying continuous model.

This study addresses geometric programming challenges through the development of an MM algorithm, facilitated by an upper-level surrogate objective function that simplifies its solution process. The application of this approach yields efficient and numerically precise algorithms for solving both signomial and geometric programming problems, with a time efficiency of O(n^3) and an error tolerance on the order of several epsilon values multiplied by the problem's parameters.

The Teichmüller space Teich, defined as the set of isotopy classes of metrics on a surface, can be viewed in two distinct ways. Firstly, it is essentially the space of holomorphic maps from the surface to the unit disk. Secondly, the space naturally arises from the space of holomorphic mappings from the surface to the complex projective line, equipped with a certain measure. In this alternative form, the space Teich is a fundamental component in the theory of complex dynamics. This paper explores the relationship between these two perspectives, with an emphasis on the ergodic theory aspect of Teichmüller space.

We introduce a novel approach to generating highly realistic, non-fitting implicit neural avatars from a single video sequence captured by an RGB-D camera. This method empowers us to learn and optimize the shape and appearance of an individual without requiring any prior data or specific equipment, such as multiple cameras or motion tracking devices. Our technique leverages a novel neural rendering concept, combining an implicit neural representation for pose estimation and an implicit neural renderer for appearance calculation. We train our model using a series of optimized loss functions, including a novel loss that enables accurate registration of an avatar to a captured video without any pre-calculations or intermediate representations. Our results demonstrate that this method can learn accurate, high-fidelity neural avatars from a single video, showcasing its effectiveness across various subjects and environments.

A novel approach has been developed to remove occlusions from faces in images using a combination of a 3D model-based method and a neural network. This two-stage process first estimates a subject's underlying facial structure from a partially obscured image, and subsequently utilizes a generative neural network to recreate the complete face. To refine this process, the network is trained with a regularization technique that incorporates a 3D model-based loss function. Experimental evaluations on several datasets, including the CelebA dataset, demonstrate significant improvements in de-occluded face quality when compared to single-stage methods, and rival those of existing state-of-the-art solutions.

Machine learning has seen a significant shift from purely supervised learning to the integration of reinforcement learning and imitation learning. However, traditional approaches often struggle to adapt to real-world environments, which are inherently complex and uncertain. To overcome these limitations, researchers have been actively exploring the potential of intrinsic motivation as an alternative to traditional loss functions. By focusing on the intrinsic rewards that arise from interacting with the environment, agents can learn more efficiently and effectively. This brief introduction aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art research in intrinsic motivated reinforcement learning, highlighting its key concepts, challenges, and future research directions.

In a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning environment, we examine the convergence of a distributed policy iteration algorithm where local agents adjust their policies based on neighboring interactions. We prove that this localized approach converges globally provided the communication network is connected, without imposing any restrictions on the policy update step. Furthermore, our analysis yields a quantitative measure for the rate of convergence. Building on this, we investigate the scenario where local policy updates are executed at discrete time intervals, with a fixed delay between networked agent interactions. Under the condition that the combined network connectivity and delay satisfies a modified criterion, we show that the distributed policy iteration algorithm converges, with a delay-dependent rate of convergence.

Researchers have conducted a study on two-jet events in high-energy proton-proton collisions, focusing on the significant gap in rapidity between the leading jets. The gap in rapidity between the jets, denoted as Δη* and exceeding 2, was used as the primary distinguishing feature of events. The data collected with the CMS detector at a 13-millibarn cross-section, equivalent to 5.35 inverse femtobarns of data, revealed that the observed dijet patterns match predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics. The findings also suggest that diffractive and non-diffractive processes occur with comparable probabilities.

Silicon, a widely used material in the semiconductor industry, has a previously unreported allotrope called penta-silicene, a silicon-based nanomaterial. Research has shown that penta-silicene possesses exceptional electronic, thermal, and mechanical characteristics, making it a strong candidate for use in thermoelectric devices. By analyzing its electronic and thermal transport properties, it was found that penta-silicene has the potential to achieve a high power efficiency. The material's natural ability to maintain its electronic properties under stress also makes it suitable for use in thermoelectric applications. Theoretical models have predicted that penta-silicene has the potential to achieve a high power efficiency of 6.59 at room temperature, making it a promising candidate for the development of high-performance thermoelectric materials.

The fractional nonrelativistic potential model is employed to investigate the dissociation of heavy quarkonia in a magnetized, hot environment. Building upon the nonrelativistic potential model, the fractional differential equation is derived and solved using the differential correction method. To account for the influence of a magnetized environment, the obtained bound state solutions are adjusted to incorporate the magnetic field's effect. Subsequently, the thermal influence is incorporated by considering the system as interacting with a heat bath and introducing the thermal energy into the system. To achieve this, the differential correction method is applied to the fractional differential equation, yielding the dissociation temperature of heavy quarkonia in a magnetized, hot medium. The obtained results are then compared with existing experimental data.

The universe is thought to hold vast amounts of dark matter in small, leftover structures from galaxy formation.  Particle colliders and other experiments may not be the only tools capable of detecting this remaining dark matter.  Other key candidates for uncovering dark matter include old stars and cosmic radiation.  In this study, we examine the potential for dark matter subhalos to be discovered through interactions with neutron stars and cosmic radiation.  Our calculations involve a general model for subhalos and their interaction cross sections, and we consider various types of particles that could make up the dark matter.  Our results show that the detection threshold for these particles is relatively low, and we estimate the potential for detecting dark matter subhalos in these scenarios.  Our estimates suggest that the detection threshold is relatively low, and we estimate the potential for detecting dark matter subhalos in these scenarios.  Our study suggests that the detection threshold is within reach for experiments involving neutron stars and cosmic radiation.  In particular, we estimate that the potential for detecting dark matter subhalos in neutron star interactions could be significant, with a potential detection threshold in the milligravities range.  Our study also suggests that the potential for detecting dark matter subhalos in cosmic radiation interactions could be substantial, with a potential detection threshold in the range of kiloelectronvolts. In our research, we examine a mixed patrolling and signaling strategy used by gamekeepers to manage wildlife conservation areas with human activity. These individuals must balance the risk of being seen by humans while maintaining their safety and the integrity of the area. Our objective is to optimize the gamekeepers' behavior to minimize the risk of human encounters while minimizing gamekeeper movements. This problem is complex due to its Markov decision process nature, the lack of immediate rewards, and the human agents' unpredictable behavior. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that combines reinforcement learning and Bayesian estimation to model the human behavior and develop an efficient gamekeeping policy. Our approach is evaluated on a large synthetic game environment and outperforms existing methods in terms of both performance and computational complexity.

Deep reinforcement learning has been successfully applied to various robotic tasks, but its performance can be compromised in real-world scenarios due to the complexity and uncertainty in outdoor environments. This study focuses on addressing the challenges posed by uneven terrain and developing a reliable navigation system for mobile robots. The proposed method, termed terrain-aware exploration and control policy (TERP), utilizes a deep reinforcement learning framework to learn an optimal navigation policy in such environments. The TERP method incorporates a novel terrain-aware reward structure, which combines rewards for reaching the goal and avoiding obstacles to encourage informed agent behavior. Additionally, it introduces a novel exploration strategy to effectively navigate uneven terrain. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the TERP method in navigating uneven environments compared to existing state-of-the-art navigation methods.

A simulation of a system consisting of dipolar hard spheres was performed, and the results indicate the presence of a phase transition at a specific concentration, approximately 0.475 volume fraction. This value was found to be consistent with results obtained using alternative methods, such as critical analysis via the Ising star and a mean-field approximation model.

This research tackles the inverse problem of determining the conductivity in a planar object that is insulated. Given the potential to measure the voltage and current flowing across the object from its boundaries, the goal is to develop methods for estimating the conductivity from these measurements. This is a complex task due to the non-linearity of the conductivity distribution and the limited information available from boundary measurements, which can result in edge effects. Furthermore, the properties of the conductivity include singularities and boundaries, making it difficult to analyze. This study proposes a mathematical approach to address this problem by using the properties of the gradient of the single layer potential to develop new methods.

We investigate the stability of toroidal magnetic fields within stars under the assumption that their magnetic parameters remain constant, through the application of the Babcock and Parker model. We derive a necessary stability criterion for these fields, extending the classic Taylor-Parker criterion, and then proceed to analyze the stability of the field under ideal conditions in the presence of axial symmetry. We derive a necessary stability criterion for these fields, extending the classic Taylor-Parker criterion, and then embark on the stability analysis of the field under ideal conditions in the presence of axial symmetry.

This research delves into the intricate relationships between the underlying graph structure, the topology of the network, and its dynamic behavior. Specifically, it examines how these factors impact the system's convergence speed during the process of simplicial synchronization. Our findings indicate that geometric properties of the graph play a crucial role in determining the speed of convergence. To quantify this effect, we developed a novel metric called the geometric deviation, which captures the impact of graph geometry on the synchronization process. Our theoretical analysis is supported by computational experiments, which validate the importance of graph geometry and the effectiveness of our proposed convergence metric.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication, a fundamental operation in scientific computing, is a performance-critical component of iterative linear solvers. As such, enhancing the SpMV, often through the use of precomputed cache blocks, has become a well-established practice, yet there remains a need to investigate novel strategies for optimization. This article surveys the existing body of knowledge on SpMV optimization techniques, focusing on the application of hierarchical matrices, which offer a balance between computational efficiency and SpMV performance, and provide insights into the effectiveness of iterative solvers. It also explores the use of cache hierarchy and parallelization as complementary methods to boost SpMV performance.

Suppose we have two collections of meromorphic functions on a specific domain and a non-zero complex number. It can be proven that if functions in the first set are relatively compex hyperbolic equivalent to a certain type of normal functions within the same domain, and these normal functions also relate to a second collection of functions through some shared values, then the functions in the first set are also normal within the same domain.

Our goal is to create a reliable and efficient system for accurately detecting a user's intentions when they point with a device, to enhance the functionality of head-mounted displays with intuitive gesture recognition. Current AR head-mounted devices require users to select objects by pointing, but this method can be slow and frustrating, so we've developed a system to recognize pointing intentions, which can then initiate object selection more efficiently. We've tested our method, called HAIR, in a controlled study and found that it outperforms existing approaches in precision, speed, and accuracy, with the added benefit of being resistant to glare.

Monge-Amp\`ere systems can be represented as a set of coupled nonlinear PDEs, and they naturally appear in various fields such as geometry, mechanics, and physics. These systems are often linked to a Lagrangian system in a dual space. Our study reveals that in dual spaces, Monge-Amp\`ere systems are equivalent to Lagrangian Hamiltonian systems. Building on this insight, we develop a method to derive a modified version of the Mather transformation for these systems in their original space. This method is applied to a specific system, yielding a novel Poincaré recurrence theorem.

This study explores the influence of natural convection on the evolution of gas bubbles attached to electrodes, taking into account the effects of surface tension and mass transport. A new model is developed to describe the bubble's shape and size by considering the forces at play, including surface tension, buoyancy, inertia, and viscous forces. The model is then applied to understand how natural convection affects the growth and dissolution of bubbles in electrode processes like limiting current and bubble evolution/dissolution within cavities. The results reveal that convection can speed up the growth of spherical or hemispherical bubbles, but slow down the growth of hemispherical bubbles attached to electrodes at certain angles. This phenomenon is particularly significant in certain electrode processes, like limiting current, where it can lead to bubble detachment and even dissolution at specific current densities. On the other hand, convection accelerates the dissolution of bubbles in a linear fashion, regardless of their shape, and can cause bubble detachment in certain electrode processes, like corrosion, which can lead to the formation of gas pockets.

A 2016-2017 study involving 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC explored the possibility of particles with extended lifetimes producing high-energy photons. This study utilized a data set of 77.2 fb^-1, which was recorded using the CMS detector, to determine the maximum and average lifetimes of these particles. The study incorporated a unique photon timing identifier and a data-driven method to distinguish genuine photons from those produced by particles with extended lifetimes. The study's findings were compared to various theoretical models, including those of additional Higgs bosons, long-lived charginos, and heavy neutralinos.

We investigate the effects of Coulomb interactions on two types of second-order Dirac semimetals, specifically the spinless and spin-symmetric models, within mean-field approximation. The mean-field approach enables us to calculate the self-energy, self-consistently solve for the renormalized vertex function, and examine the stability of the semimetal state. Our analysis reveals that, for small interaction strengths, the spin-symmetric model exhibits a logarithmic correction to the Semenoff state, whereas the spinless model displays a power-law correction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical line separating the Semenoff and normal states for the spin-symmetric model is linear, differing from the quadratic behavior observed in isotropic Dirac semimetals.

Developing concurrent code is notoriously challenging due to the constant need
to balance concurrent processes with data safety requirements. One strategy to
overcome this hurdle involves inferring concurrent code implementations from
formal specifications. However, current inference techniques fall short as they
rely on sequential abstractions, failing to account for the complexities of
concurrent code. In contrast, our research presents a novel approach that utilizes
logic-based inference to derive concurrent code from sequential data structures,
resulting in more accurate and efficient implementations.

Researchers have proposed using advanced levitation technology to conduct highly sensitive experiments that can detect and analyze subtle changes in gravity and vibrations using super-polished microspheres in unique vacuum environments. This research presents a new approach to such experiments, utilizing a microsphere suspended on a magnetically-actuated oscillating platform, which allows for precise frequency tuning and efficient energy dissipation. This method is particularly suitable for low-frequency and high-sensitivity applications, such as monitoring minute gravitational waves, and can be easily integrated with existing technology, such as commercial nanoCopter systems.

We've identified two new forms of a molecular compound, specifically 3-cyclopentadienyl-yclopropenyl acetylene and cyclopropenyl cyclopentadiene acetylene, within a specific region of space called TMC-1. These discoveries were facilitated by the detection of their unique molecular structures using advanced technology that can identify specific types of compounds. We've also identified the most abundant forms of acetylene and cyanide molecules within cyclopentadiene and cyclopropenyl cyclopentadiene. Our analysis of the data suggests that compounds containing acetylene and cyanide are relatively rare within these specific molecular environments.

A novel framework for asymmetric dark matter is presented with a gravitational wave origin. In this framework, primordial black holes emit gravitational waves, which create a dark matter-dark matter-dark matter interaction, leading to the formation of a subdominant dark matter population. This subdominant population can then generate the dominant dark matter through a self-interaction process. In contrast to traditional self-interaction-driven dark matter formation, this framework offers a solution to the small-scale structure problem without introducing new free parameters. The framework's key advantage lies in its ability to produce a smooth, continuous dark matter profile in small-scale regions. The feasibility of this framework is explored in two distinct scenarios: one involving a monochromatic gravitational wave spectrum and the other featuring a broad-spectrum emission.

Using 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, the ATLAS experiment measured the associated production cross-section of a $t\bar{t}Z$ in the 4$\ell$ channel. The observed $t\bar{t}Z$ candidates were selected based on three or more charged leptons, missing transverse momentum, and at least 75 GeV in missing transverse momentum and 20 GeV in transverse momentum for the Z boson candidate. The $t\bar{t}Z$ candidates were identified by the presence of two jets, two leptons, and neutrinos from top-quark decay, while the Z boson decay was identified through an e-e, $\mu\mu$, or $\tau\tau$ final state. The measured $t\bar{t}Z$ production cross-section was 1.07 pb, with an uncertainty of 0.46 pb for the statistical uncertainty, 0.16 pb for the systematic uncertainty, and 0.4 pb for the luminosity uncertainty. This result agreed with the predicted Standard Model cross-section of 93.2 pb with a uncertainty of 6. 0 pb.

We have made advancements in the classification of four-qubit states composed of rebits, which are two-state particles and the most basic units in a phase space with non-binary properties similar to a qubit. The study of these states is valuable for its potential in quantum information processing and for its role in understanding the properties of non-binary Hilbert spaces. In this research, we have developed a method to categorize rebit states using a mathematical concept called the real Pauli exclusive OR gates. Our findings show that the dynamics of real Pauli exclusive OR gates can be used to classify states with three and four particles, and that these operators have a direct relationship with the properties of four-qubit stabilizer states. We have also discovered that the classification of states with four particles is connected to the properties of non-binary Hilbert spaces, specifically that the Pauli exclusive OR gates form a complete set of operators for these spaces.

Predictive state representations are a type of abstract state space derived from high-dimensional systems' future behavior. They have a notable advantage in that they don't need to be learned through machine learning and can be used in combination with established reinforcement learning methods. However, predictive state representations have a limitation: they don't support a method for estimating the current state based on rewards. As a result, predictive state representations have been limited to applications in model-based reinforcement learning, despite their potential for broader use. To address this, we have developed a method for estimating the current state based on rewards using predictive state representations. This method involves using a neural network to approximate the current state based on past rewards and then using a predictive state representation to determine the abstract state. Our approach is unique because it doesn't require the high-dimensional system to be learned through machine learning and can be used in conjunction with established reinforcement learning methods. Our experiments have shown that our method can effectively learn state representations for complex systems and improve learning efficiency.

This research examines the development of a gentrification early warning system by exploring the factors that contribute to gentrification and assessing their spatial variability within a metropolitan area. To create a comprehensive model, we combine various approaches, including using machine learning to analyze spatial data and identifying patterns in gentrification through social network analysis. These methods are integrated to create a gentrification risk assessment tool that considers the interplay between neighborhood characteristics and changes to the social fabric. The development of this tool utilizes a collaborative approach, incorporating input from diverse stakeholders in Buffalo, New York. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a framework for the creation of data-driven, community-driven gentrification early warning systems that inform public policy and foster public awareness.

In chiral magnets, skyrmion crystals can be stabilized by a specific type of spin order. We investigated the properties of a specific type of chiral magnet, Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, using X-ray diffraction and magnetic force microscopy to study its magnetic behavior. At room temperature, the material exhibits a specific type of spin order that is typical of certain chiral magnets, but it undergoes a phase transition at 25 K to form a skyrmion crystal. Our results show that the skyrmion crystal remains stable down to 3.5 K, but we observed a unique type of melting transition that is not previously observed in other chiral magnets. The skyrmion crystal undergoes a first-order melting transition that is characterized by the formation of smaller skyrmions, followed by a topological correction that restores the equilibrium skyrmion size. This topological correction is a rare phenomenon in the field of topological magnetism and is likely to be a general feature of certain types of chiral magnets.

This study examines composition operators within the realm of Harmonic-Bloch type spaces and computes the spectrum for these operators, also identifying isometric composition operators in harmonic Bloch type spaces.

The integration of electric vehicles into urban transportation systems is a significant step towards reducing greenhouse gas emissions. To optimize the process, various routing strategies have been developed for electric vehicles. Nevertheless, the limitations of electric vehicles' range force many trips to be completed using fossil fuel-based vehicles, leading to increased emissions. This study presents a novel routing approach that combines electric and conventional vehicles, aiming to minimize costs while reducing emissions. The proposed method, based on an agent model, allocates trips to electric vehicles, maximizing their range usage. The model also determines the optimal number of electric vehicles and trip assignments for both electric and conventional vehicles, maximizing savings. The proposed method, applied to a large network of 170 nodes, demonstrates a 25% reduction in emissions when compared to conventional trips and a 2.5% reduction in overall costs.

We investigate the light-front distribution amplitudes of heavy mesons, specifically those of the bottom and charm quarks, within the context of the light-front quark model. By employing the instant-form T-matrix formalism, we calculate the values of several key non-perturbative distribution amplitudes, including the first five Gegenbauer coefficients, and compare our results to existing lattice QCD data and experimental findings. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the bottom quark-related amplitudes, utilizing the bottom quark's first two excited states as a means of deriving a relationship between the bottom quark's alpha parameter and its mass.

This paper investigates the a priori error analysis for stabilised Enhanced Velocity methods used to solve transient advection-diffusion problems in the discrete-time environment. The methods are based on unstructured grids and incorporate the CVT Petrov-Galerkin scheme, which replaces the conventional time discretisation method. By examining the CVT scheme's approximation properties, we establish improved approximation properties for the transient Enhanced Velocity scheme. Notably, we demonstrate that the scheme achieves optimal second-order accuracy in spatial directions and first-order accuracy in time. An a posteriori error analysis is also provided, highlighting the features of the transient Enhanced Velocity method.

Deep learning has revolutionized the field of autonomous driving, enabling the development of efficient and accurate models for analyzing spatial video data. However, effectively training these models requires high-quality training datasets, which are challenging to create and maintain. A more practical approach involves leveraging existing video data sets and utilizing models pre-trained on them, a strategy that is particularly beneficial for tasks requiring large-scale training datasets. A key factor in making this approach successful lies in integrating the models with geoinformation systems, enabling the precise selection of video data sets based on the specific needs of the driving environment. A driving context model, which incorporates both models and data, has been proposed to address these challenges. This approach enables the identification of relevant data sets and models, as well as their applications, utilizing a geospatial data infrastructure. A proof-of-concept implementation demonstrates the feasibility of this approach, highlighting its potential to facilitate the creation of efficient and accurate models for autonomous driving applications.

The behavior of GaN MESFETs under high illumination conditions has been analyzed, focusing on the impact of photoionization on the device's electrical properties. A two-dimensional model has been developed to simulate the device's electrical characteristics under light exposure, considering both the generation of carriers and the ionization of existing traps within the device. The model has been successfully compared to experimental results, demonstrating its accuracy in predicting the device's electrical performance under different illumination levels. The findings show that the device's electrical properties are significantly affected by trap ionization, resulting in the formation of negative space-charge layers. These layers cause a decrease in the device's drain current and a positive shift in the device's threshold voltage.

This study introduces a particle filter-based approach to develop a reliable GNSS positioning method that resists the detrimental effects of various faulty GNSS signals. To counter potential signal interference, a novel cost function is formulated to evaluate the performance of each GNSS receiver. The proposed method incorporates a cost function tailored to each receiver, allowing it to detect and isolate faulty GNSS signals. To ensure accurate positioning, a cost function is also defined for the positioning solution, which is then used to determine the most reliable set of GNSS signals and to solve the positioning problem with guaranteed accuracy. A simulation study demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method in the presence of various levels and types of signal interference, showing that it achieves more accurate positioning compared to traditional methods.

A novel tensor graphical model, SG-PALM, is introduced that efficiently learns the physical connections within high-dimensional data sets derived from tensor sensor readings. SG-PALM is designed to provide rapid and accurate estimations of tensor data's underlying network, which in turn enable the identification of the relationships between the variables, their partial dependence, and total dependence, all while maintaining a computationally efficient and scalable framework. Experimental results demonstrate that SG-PALM outperforms state-of-the-art tensor graphical models in terms of both speed and the quality of the resulting network, with its implementation available online at the specified GitHub repository.

This study explores using event-based cameras to count moving objects, a task typically difficult to perform with conventional cameras, especially when objects are in motion. The researchers developed an innovative method to track objects by tracking clusters of sensor activations in the camera's frame. The approach starts by training a neural network to identify clusters of interest. The network then generates a set of reference vectors that represent these clusters. The camera's sensor data is then segmented into clusters. The researchers then calculate the size of each cluster and track its movement over time. If a cluster disappears, it is considered a new object entering the field of view. Conversely, if a cluster's size remains constant while moving, it is considered an object moving within the field of view. The researchers tested their approach using an event-based camera to track a moving object through a series of obstacles. The results showed that their method was able to accurately track the object's presence or absence at a rate of 100 frames per second, with an average error of 0.5%.

This research paper focuses on maximizing throughput in hybrid network-cached, multi-level cache-enabled heterogeneous networks. A novel approach to throughput maximization in these networks has been proposed, where cache placement is optimized to enhance transmission efficiency. Initially, the network's topology is optimized through an algorithm, and then the cache content is determined based on network characteristics and user requirements. Specifically, the problem is framed as a mixed-integer programming problem, and an efficient solution algorithm is developed to address it. Additionally, the study explores the challenges of throughput maximization in these networks, and demonstrates that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in achieving higher throughput and lower complexity.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented, which involves the classification of bipartite states. A significant outcome of this research is the proof of the PPT square conjecture for bipartite states with a dimension of 3 or lower. Furthermore, this conjecture is proven for bipartite pure states with a specific property, and the possibility of entanglement in these states is explored. Additionally, this study examines the PPT square conjecture for a specific class of bipartite states and presents an approach for breaking the PPT square limit, resulting in the creation of a bipartite state from two mixed ones.

A certain type of transitive Cayley graphs, specifically those with normal edges, are investigated to determine specific criteria that categorize them as a normal edge-transitive Cayley graph. Additionally, the necessary requirements for a group to be a normal edge-transitive base group of a normal edge-transitive Cayley graph are analyzed. Furthermore, the properties of a subgroup, referred to as a Frattini-like subgroup, which has the potential to generate a normal edge-transitive Cayley graph are examined. Several examples of normal edge-transitive Cayley graphs, including those that arise from certain finite groups and their corresponding Frattini-like subgroups, are provided.

The relationship between shear modulus and electron density in jellium is used to make predictions about the elastic properties of metals under high pressure. Using a theoretical model, values for the bulk and shear modulus are calculated, along with their corresponding modulus anisotropies. These calculated bulk and shear moduli are then compared to experimental results and other theoretical models to assess their accuracy.

Blurring caused by camera movement in videos is a common issue, which can be addressed by video deblurring techniques. However, these methods often struggle to distinguish between human figures and the background, which can lead to poor deblurring results. To overcome this challenge, a novel approach is proposed that separates the scene into layers and uses a neural network to synthesize blurred segments. The method involves a two-stage process: first, it identifies human and background regions, and second, it generates synthetic blurred frames to aid deblurring. The method is evaluated on a dataset of real blurred videos, which were previously deblurred using synthetic blur, and compared to ground truth images. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving higher deblurring accuracy and lower computation time.

The occurrence of tidal disruption events, where a star is consumed by a supermassive black hole, can lead to the generation of electromagnetic and gravitational waves, offering a means of discovering black holes. However, not all transient luminosities are attributed to tidal disruptions; other celestial and non-celestial sources can produce similar effects. To distinguish between genuine tidal disruptions and impostors, researchers have developed a new approach. By combining the black hole's mass and the outburst's luminosity, a distinct boundary can be established, which is influenced by the outburst's duration. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations of tidal disruptions and the analysis of 136 such events, along with 55 impostors. The results show that the approach accurately distinguishes between genuine tidal disruptions and the majority of impostors.

Our research reveals the presence of dense galaxy clusters surrounding 14 out of 31 highly luminous Lyman-alpha emitters observed with the Keck-MOSFIRE spectrograph at an age equivalent to z = 6.6. These clusters are composed of multiple Lyman-alpha emitters with velocities clustered within a small range, consistent with a group or cluster environment. Notably, their presence was not anticipated given the small volume probed. By comparing the observed data with a simulation model, we found that the distribution of these dense clusters matches the average density of galaxies at this age. However, they are significantly more common than predicted by the simulation, with a 4.3 times higher occurrence rate. This discrepancy may be attributed to the simulation's limitations in reproducing the large-scale structure of the universe at this age. Alternatively, the observed dense clusters could be comprised of multiple, closely spaced Lyman-alpha emitters.

A comprehensive study of the reflectance spectra of 21 cold classical TNOs has been conducted, covering a wavelength range of 0.45 to 0.92 micrometers. Our sample of 21 objects, including 17 previously unstudied TNOs, includes a diverse set of cold classical and hot population TNOs, as well as two objects from the Scattered Disc. Our analysis revealed that 16 objects exhibited a reddish spectrum, while three objects showed a more neutral color. By comparing our data to existing TNO observations, we were able to determine that these objects are likely to be less active and less diverse in their composition than hot population TNOs. Our findings also suggest that these objects are less suitable for targeted surveys, but are better suited to all-sky observations.

The cold dwell phenomenon is a critical factor in the design and development of titanium alloys used in aerospace and other industries. This behavior, characterized by significant creep and stress relaxation, is influenced by various factors including alloy composition, temperature, and loading conditions. In this study, the impact of the cold dwell effect is investigated in Ti$_6$Al alloys subjected to uniaxial tension, with a focus on understanding load shedding and the associated strain and stress distributions. Load shedding is observed during the cold dwell phase, and it is shown that this effect can be predicted using the Taylor-Larson effect, which accounts for the increasing size of primary slip systems during deformation.

Software product lines consist of a large set of software engineering artifacts that are interrelated, which can be effectively managed using feature models to account for the inclusion or exclusion of certain features.  However, feature models can be complex and difficult to understand, which can hinder their use in software product line engineering.  In order to gain a better understanding of how developers interpret feature models, an empirical study was conducted involving feature model diagrams with varying levels of complexity.  The results of this study indicate that certain diagram components are more easily comprehended than others, and that feature model clarity can be improved by employing specific organizational strategies.

Astronomers have been using high-contrast imaging techniques to identify and study faint companions surrounding stars for nearly a century, but recent breakthroughs in adaptive optics technology have led to a surge in discoveries. Consequently, there is now a pressing need for more efficient detection methods that can process the vast amounts of data generated by these instruments. To address this challenge, a new pipeline called StraKLIP has been developed, building on the Karhunen-Loéve Image Processing algorithm. This pipeline utilizes a machine learning approach to optimize the analysis of high-sensitivity detectors, such as the Hubble Space Telescope's WFC3/105 instrument, and has been optimized for detecting low-mass stars and exoplanets in the vicinity of bright stars. When tested on a sample of 20 stars observed with HST/ACS, StraKLIP successfully detected all known companions and identified 12 additional candidates, of which 6 were later confirmed through spectroscopic analysis. StraKLIP's effectiveness has been demonstrated by successfully detecting companions as faint as those in the HST sample, and its ability to identify even fainter companions. This makes it a powerful tool for detecting close-in faint companions and characterizing their properties.

We examine a simplified model of the Page scenario, specifically the collapse of a black hole into two equal mass objects, to investigate the impact of various symmetries on the Page curve. Our findings indicate that the specific point at which the Page boundary is reached can be influenced by the presence of certain symmetries, such as translation or boost invariance, by varying the Page time. However, for single-particle states with no residual entropy, our analysis shows that the Page boundary remains unchanged under different unitary evolutions, as determined by the approach to thermalization. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the Page boundary remains robust against small perturbations in the entanglement of the collapsing object.

We demonstrate a method to reconstruct fermionic properties in artificial materials by manipulating energy levels. Our results show that in a lattice with a non-trivial topological structure, the energy levels can be adjusted to mimic the behavior of Fermi arcs - unique arcs of stability in these complex systems. Through precise calculations, we identify the conditions required to replicate Fermi arcs in these artificial materials, and our research offers a roadmap for creating novel topological phases in optically based artificial crystals.

Our proposed method tackles the challenge of long-term, complex video prediction, 
achieving impressive results even when the target objects are outside the training 
domain. This is made possible by combining two key components: a hierarchical 
approach that divides the video into manageable, fine-grained segments, and a 
novel, unsupervised method for estimating object motion. By applying this 
approach to a well-established short-term video prediction model, we're able to 
significantly outperform the state-of-the-art models on the challenging EPIC-KITCHENS 
benchmark, even in unseen domains.

The dual role of mitochondria, involving the energy production necessary for cellular life and the initiation of programmed cell death in certain situations, highlights the complex nature of these organelles.  Research has shown that the genetic makeup of mitochondria, influenced by mutations such as those seen in a common form of blindness, can change over time.  The factors that contribute to these changes are not yet fully understood, despite ongoing research efforts.  This study investigates the impact of mitochondrial structure on the genetic behavior of these organelles, using a unique approach that combines computational models with experimental methods to study the genetic exchange between mitochondria in human cells.  The findings suggest that the genetic makeup of mitochondria is influenced by the connections between them, with the location of mitochondria in the cell affecting the rate at which genetic mutations occur.  This study provides new insights into the factors that contribute to mitochondrial genetic mutations, shedding light on a previously unexplored aspect of these processes.

We introduce Mixer-TTS, a non-autoregressive text-to-speech model that leverages language model embeddings for speech generation. Mixer-TTS is unique among its peers due to several innovative features: Firstly, it employs cross-image attention for efficient speech synthesis, diverging from the conventional mel-spectrogram objective. Secondly, the model is designed to be non-autoregressive, enabling the generation of speech in a single forward pass. Thirdly, Mixer-TTS exhibits remarkable compactness, requiring merely 35.8 million parameters to achieve high-quality speech synthesis. Notably, the model attains a TTS quality score of 0.39 on the MOS@8th task while outperforming state-of-the-art non-autoregressive models by a substantial margin, using a mere fraction of the parameters.

The ternary alloy Ge2Sb2Te5, a key component in phase-change optical storage, has been extensively researched due to its high promise in non-volatile memory. Despite this potential, the underlying mechanism of phase changes, however, remains poorly understood. This study employs a range of techniques including X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and spectroscopy to investigate the structural and electronic changes associated with these phase transitions. The results show that the material undergoes a crystalline-to-amorphous transformation, characterized by a non-reversible change in the material's structure. The material's amorphous state exhibits a high degree of disorder, with Ge and Sb atoms forming irregular networks, while Te atoms form long chains. The material's optical properties, including the material's band gap and optical absorption, change significantly during this transition. The material's amorphous state exhibits a high degree of disorder, with Ge and Sb atoms forming irregular networks, while Te atoms form long chains. The material's optical properties, including the material's band gap and optical absorption, change significantly during this transition.

We have developed a comprehensive theory to explain the unique characteristics of oblique topological insulators, which are distinct from standard topological insulators. These compounds have a 2D structure consisting of a square lattice, featuring alternating spin-orbit coupling and inversion symmetry breaking, resulting in a specific rotational symmetry of order 4. Our theory shows that oblique topological insulators exhibit a number of unusual properties, including a Z2 topological phase, a specific pattern of energy band structure, and a unique set of surface states, which are different from those found in standard topological insulators. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the surface states of oblique topological insulators are not confined to the direction of the 4-fold rotation axis but can also appear in the transverse direction. We have also identified a specific type of material, which we believe has the potential to be the first experimental realization of an oblique topological insulator.

The discovery of variations in the transmission of light from exoplanets has significant implications for understanding the atmospheric and orbital characteristics of these planets. We investigated how gaps in the protoplanetary discs of TRAPPIST-1 and K2-22, two exoplanet systems, affect the transmission spectrum of these exoplanets. Our findings suggest that large gaps in the disc can cause significant variations in the transmission spectrum, particularly for large gap openings. Furthermore, we discovered that the distribution of dust within the gap can also impact the transmission spectrum, resulting in distinct features. We also analyzed the effects of gap depth, width, and location on the transmission spectrum, and found that the transmission spectrum of TRAPPIST-1 would be significantly affected by a gap within the protoplanetary disc, particularly if the gap is located near the planet's orbital radius, resulting in a deep blue edge.

Reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world applications often faces significant challenges due to its high sample complexity. To address this issue, we propose a novel RL approach that leverages a neural network's internal representation to identify more informative next-state candidates from a set of potential options. By utilizing a neural network's hidden states as indicators of an agent's knowledge, we develop a method to select the most informative candidate with the highest corresponding knowledge score. This approach is based on the assumption that an agent's knowledge is directly tied to its ability to make informed decisions. We formalize this connection by introducing a 'knowledge score' that reflects an agent's ability to make accurate predictions about its environment. By optimizing this knowledge score, the agent learns to identify more accurate next-state candidates, thereby reducing the number of environmental interactions required to reach its target state. To achieve this goal, we propose a 'Knowledge-driven Learning Framework' that utilizes a knowledge-based loss function to optimize the knowledge score. This framework is divided into two stages: an exploration stage where the agent learns to identify more accurate next-state candidates, and a refinement stage where the agent further optimizes its knowledge score through targeted learning. To ensure that the agent's internal representation is accurate, we propose a contrastive loss function that encourages the agent to learn a more informative internal representation. This approach is demonstrated to be effective in our experimental results, where we show that our method significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art RL approaches in terms of sample efficiency

This study introduces DiaNet, a cutting-edge NLP system that utilizes hierarchical attention and multi-task learning to identify specific dialects. Our proposed model leverages BERT as its foundation and achieves state-of-the-art results in predicting dialects at a very fine-grained level. We have successfully applied DiaNet to real-world tasks such as Arabic dialect identification, text classification, and command recognition, and our experimental findings confirm its superior performance. Furthermore, our model has been put to the test in a more demanding scenario, where it accurately performed the tasks of text classification and command recognition on an unseen dialect without any prior training data.

The strip packing problem involves finding the most space-efficient way to place non-overlapping, axis-aligned rectangles within a given rectangular container, such that the container is completely filled. This problem has been shown to have a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithm, and the best known approximation factor currently stands at 1.23. In this research, we enhance the approximation factor for the specific case of Guillotine strip packing, in which the strips are restricted to having heights of 1 and 2, and find a solution with a 1.23 approximation factor.

We introduce DeepSIS, a new deep learning approach for estimating galaxy cluster masses from the Compton-y maps produced by the Planck satellite. By leveraging the power of deep learning, DeepSIS can quickly and accurately infer cluster masses without the need for computationally intensive N-body simulations or complex theoretical models. Our model was trained on simulated Compton-y maps and validated against weak lensing masses from the SPT-SZ catalog, yielding significant improvements over previous machine learning approaches. DeepSIS outperformed the previous best method by 30% in terms of mass resolution and 20% in terms of resolution bias at a fixed false positive rate. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of DeepSIS to be applied directly to the Planck Y-maps without requiring simulated data for training. Our results show that DeepSIS can accurately predict masses consistent with the SPT-SIS model for the SPT cluster sample with Compton-y values above 0.4.

The LDA model's inadequate handling of collocations poses a significant challenge when deriving semantic insights from text. A novel approach to address this limitation involves pre-processing the data by an unsupervised method that identifies and removes collocations prior to inputting the data into the LDA model. By doing so, it is possible to increase the LDA model's ability to accurately categorize text, as measured by the SILT benchmark. Moreover, this pre-processing technique yields improved results across a range of LDA models, where the benefits are most pronounced when utilizing high topic counts.

The classification of pulsars is complicated by the similarities between some pulsars and other celestial sources like supernova remnants and blazars, which complicate their identification based solely on positional and spectral data. A statistical approach called probabilistic classification is used to classify pulsars, evaluating the likelihood of each source being a pulsar, a supernova remnant, and a blazar. This method is applied to data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope and tested with known pulsars, resulting in a high accuracy rate. The method is then applied to a larger dataset and found to be effective in classifying pulsars, with minimal loss of accuracy compared to other methods. The application of probabilistic classification to astronomical data is a new and promising field that shows potential for classifying celestial sources with high accuracy rates.

We compute the Fourier and Fourier-Stieltjes algebras of Fell bundles originating from group C*-algebras, and we establish that their Fourier-Stieltjes algebras are invariant under bounded approximate identities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the unit group of the Fourier-Stieltjes algebra of a Fell bundle is isometrically isomorphic to the groupoid C*-algebra's minimal unitary group. We also provide specific conditions under which the Fourier algebra of a Fell bundle is a quasi-free algebra, and construct the C*-Hopf algebra extensions of proper and etale Fell bundles over discrete groups.

This research paper focuses on developing a method to approximate functions based on their behavior in the Hankel Sobolev space, using a unique basis derived from the prolate spheroidal wave function. This function, which is the solution to the Helmholtz equation in spherical coordinates, has far-reaching implications in various fields. The key to this method lies in establishing a tight frame, which is then used to create a practical and efficient approximation technique for functions in the Hankel Sobolev space, using a basis derived from the prolate spheroidal wave function. The paper also explores the relationship between the Hankel Sobolez space and other well-studied function spaces.

A novel method for generating atomic structures using a denoising process inspired by scores is presented, which produces high-quality atomic structures in both crystalline and disordered states. The proposed approach relies on a trained generator that produces atomic structures conditioned on a noise vector and a score output from a denoiser network, resulting in a lower energy state. The generator learns the shape of a desired atomic structure from a denoiser trained to produce a low energy score for a specific atomic configuration. The results demonstrate that our approach can produce a range of atomic structures in both crystalline and disordered states with accurate atomic arrangements, including for complex systems such as the Al-Ni-Co system, particularly for smaller atomic configurations.

The Lagrangian approach has a significant advantage in studying ocean transport and mixing compared to the Eulerian method. By simulating the movement of particles, it provides a dynamic representation of transport and mixing processes. This chapter will examine the use of Lagrangian tools in oceanography, focusing on the development of a transport-mixing framework that incorporates both diffusive and advective mixing processes. This framework will be applied to a significant ocean region, and the potential applications of Lagrangian tools in ocean monitoring, such as tracking the path of marine debris, will also be explored.

Our analysis of thermodynamic scaling in polymeric glass-forming liquids reveals
that it can be effectively explained by considering the equilibrium melting
temperature and the second and fourth order transition temperatures as critical
reference points for temperature scaling. These reference temperatures are
determined by equilibrium melting temperature and the temperatures at which
fourth-order transitions occur in the modified Sinai model and by using the
equation of state and entropy theory framework to describe the temperature
dependence of thermodynamic properties.
This paper introduces a new semi-discrete form of the modified Camassa-Holm equation with a linear dispersion term, which can be completely analyzed using the Bäcklund transformation.

This research explores the concept of contextuality in quantum mechanics within the framework of an extended quantum theory proposed by de Broglie and Bohm, which was influenced by Bell's ideas. In this approach, particles possess definite properties independent of measurement and have inherent memory of their past interactions. We have identified a previously overlooked aspect of this contextuality, which arises from the particles' internal states. This specific contextuality is a characteristic unique to the proposed extension of quantum theory and can be measured experimentally.

The study of gravastar and boson star properties has garnered significant interest, and researchers have employed various methods to explore their behavior. One such approach involves simulating the behavior of gravastar and boson star binaries, and this paper extends this by modeling compact binaries featuring gravastar, boson star, black hole, or neutron star components. The research focuses on how the orbital dynamics evolve over long periods, and it demonstrates that gravitational wave emission is the primary driver of these changes. The study reveals that gravitational waves can cause a gradual increase in the rate of orbital spin-down, and this rate is influenced by the spin of the compact object. The research also shows that gravitational waves can cause a gradual decrease in the orbit's eccentricity, and this decrease is more pronounced in systems with higher eccentricity. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of spin-orbit interactions in systems with high spin, and it suggests that gravitational waves can cause a gradual increase in the orbit's precession rate. The research also explores the behavior of compact binaries in which the compact object is replaced by a black hole or neutron star, and it demonstrates that gravitational waves can cause a gradual decrease in the orbit's size.

The core challenge in object detection lies in striking a balance between the accuracy of the results and the computational resources required to achieve them. A typical approach involves using a trained convolutional neural network to generate bounding boxes and associated scores. Historically, these scores have been based on classification data, but we propose a novel approach that directly trains the network to assign probabilities to the physical presence of objects within the image. By leveraging a single, end-to-end convolutional neural network that produces object bounding boxes and associated probabilities, our YOLO system outperforms more traditional multi-stage methods, while also demonstrating improved robustness to variations in image resolution and design.

The original Minho Quotation Resource was launched in 2011 with around 1,000
individuals quoted twice each, and it has since been re-released with over
1,700 individuals quoted, and more than half cited more than two times.
Additionally, a search engine was developed to make the database accessible.
As a result, the database gained popularity, and its quotes were viewed over
one hundred thousand times. The database's impact extends to social media platforms.

Decision trees and their ensembles have become essential machine learning tools, but their strengths and limitations have long been debated among researchers. This paper sheds new light on the relationship between these popular techniques and concept lattices - a less prominent but theoretically significant approach. By analyzing the relationship between decision trees/ensembles and concept lattices, we gain a deeper understanding of the inherent constraints of machine learning algorithms. This understanding allows us to refine these techniques and improve their performance. We demonstrate this by applying the concept lattice approach to enhance decision trees and ensembles with new features that optimize their operation. Our experiments, which compare decision concept lattices to decision trees and ensembles, show that this approach can significantly reduce the errors of well-established methods.

This research explores the disparity between the advancement of and application of Machine Learning (ML) methods, with a focus on the critical role of evaluation in driving innovation and understanding its limitations. Historically, ML innovation has been driven by evaluation, yet current trends in ML development often prioritize building and sharing models, rather than evaluating them thoroughly. Our study examines the current landscape of ML evaluation practices in research settings, highlighting the shift from traditional statistical methods to visual and automated evaluation tools. However, we contend that significant gaps exist between the current state of ML evaluation in research and the needs of real-world practitioners. Our analysis identifies key areas of concern, such as the lack of accessible and transparent tools, the unavailability of relevant evaluation methods, and the challenges of evaluating complex, large-scale systems. Our study also touches on the role of evaluation in addressing critical social issues, such as bias and fairness, and the importance of addressing these evaluation gaps to ensure that ML research continues to meet the needs of and benefit society.

In real-world settings, data is often characterized by power imbalance, with numerous classes having varying numbers of samples, and by rare classes with even further unequal sample distributions, and these are frequently updated with new data. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying rare classes in such power-imbalanced data, with the added complexity of emerging new classes. We introduce a new framework, called Power-ICR, that combines class sampling and prototype learning to recognize emerging rare classes. We also develop a method to estimate prototype learning uncertainty using sample density, and leverage this to dynamically adjust the prototype update process. We conduct experiments on multiple datasets to compare the performance of Power-ICR against established baselines, and observe that Power-ICR outperforms them across the board.

A significant challenge in ptychography is the limited range of object phase changes it can detect, particularly for thick samples. To overcome this issue, we have developed an alternative ptychography technique that uses a focused probe to image objects. Our approach involves using a low-probe-defocus to collect images with high spatial resolution, and then applying a phase retrieval algorithm to calculate the complex probe. We have found that our technique can effectively measure object phase changes of up to several milliradians, even in thick samples. To further improve the technique, we have also developed a new algorithm that can calculate the local atomic structure of samples using a focused probe and multiple images. Our algorithm, which uses a ptychographic diffraction pattern, can calculate the complex probe and object phase, and then applies a new phase matching algorithm to determine the local atomic structure. Our approach has been demonstrated using a 100 micron thick sample of polycrystalline aluminum, and has been shown to produce high-resolution images of individual grains. Our technique has also been applied to determine the local atomic structure of samples, and has been shown to produce high-resolution images of individual grains.
